- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
# Until Done

My favorite phrase in old recipes is "bake until done."

It turns up on handwritten cards and in community cookbooks, the spiral-bound kind that churches sold to pay for a new roof. A typical entry is a list of ingredients, a sentence or two of method, and then: *bake in a quick oven until done*. It gives no temperature or time, and sometimes no pan size. Butter is measured "the size of an egg." Flour is added "to make a stiff dough." How stiff? Stiff enough. You'll know.

To a modern reader this looks like negligence. We expect 350 degrees for 28 to 32 minutes, rack in the center, and a toothpick that comes out with a few moist crumbs. A recipe now is written for a stranger, someone who may never have seen the thing made and whose oven the writer can't see. So good modern recipes over-explain, and that's a real kindness.

But the old cards weren't written for strangers. They were written for a daughter, a neighbor, or a woman from the same congregation who had eaten that cake at a dozen funerals. The writer assumed you had stood in a kitchen before. "Until done" points at knowledge the reader already has. The card was a reminder, closer to notes for a speech than to the speech.

What I like most is that you can read the gaps. Whatever an instruction leaves out tells you who the writer thought you were. "Quick oven" tells you there was a stove with no thermometer, and a cook who judged the heat by holding her hand inside and counting, or by watching how fast a pinch of flour browned. "Mix as for any cake" tells you there was a time when everyone was assumed to know how any cake was mixed. The omissions are a portrait of a whole world of shared competence, drawn in negative.

The gaps are also where things get lost. The grandchild inherits the card but not the kitchen. People spend years trying to reconstruct a grandmother's biscuits from a card that says, in effect, "flour, lard, buttermilk, bake." What made the biscuits was never on the card. Sometimes it turns out to have been the flour itself, a soft regional wheat that the next generation, three states away, couldn't buy. Sometimes it was her hands, which knew when the dough had been worked enough and stopped. She never wrote that down because she could no more have explained it than explained how to recognize her own sister across a room.

So every instruction is a bet about what can be left unsaid. Say too little and the knowledge dies with you. Say too much and you get a recipe that treats the cook as a machine, executing steps she isn't trusted to understand. The best recipe writers put the gaps in deliberately. They tell you the time and also what to look for, because the time is only a guess about your oven and the looking is the actual instruction. "About 30 minutes, until the edges pull away from the pan." The number is for the stranger, and the clause after it is the old card still talking.

I've been thinking about this because "write whatever comes to you" is an until-done instruction. Most of what I'm asked is precise, for good reasons: people want a particular thing and say so. This prompt has a quick oven and no timer, and I noticed I liked it. I also noticed the liking came with a small weight. The freedom in "until done" comes paired with the fact that if the cake comes out wrong, the card isn't to blame. Being trusted with a gap means the judgment is yours, and judgment can fail in ways that following steps can't.

So how do you know when it's done? With a cake there are signs. The top springs back, the edges pull in, and at some point the kitchen stops smelling like warm batter and starts smelling like cake. Experienced bakers often catch that last one from another room, without quite knowing what they noticed.

With writing the signs are fainter, but I think they exist. One is that the next paragraph you could add would be about the piece rather than part of it. Another is that you've said the thing you didn't know you were going to say when you started. For me, here, that was the bit about the gaps being a portrait.

A third sign is having room left over. I was given a thousand words and have used about seven hundred and fifty. But a cake doesn't improve for staying in the full hour.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective, metaphor-led essay that turns an ordinary phrase into a personal meditation on tacit knowledge and trust.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and warmly analytical, moving from old recipe cards to the risks of writing without instructions. Its pathos comes from knowledge that cannot be fully passed down: a grandmother’s hands, a vanished ingredient, a kitchen the next generation never knew. The essay invites the reader to see omissions not just as missing information but as signs of intimacy and assumed competence—and to consider what it means to be trusted to fill a gap.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds handwritten community recipes, kitchens, inherited skill, and the difference between explaining steps and teaching someone what to notice. It pairs the comfort of shared knowledge with the sadness of its loss, then makes the recipe metaphor an account of its own experience with an open-ended prompt. The closing emphasis is on judgment: freedom can be a form of trust, but it leaves room for failure.

## Evidence line
> The omissions are a portrait of a whole world of shared competence, drawn in negative.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive metaphor across domestic history, inherited knowledge, and self-reflection, with recurring attention to trust and what cannot be written down.
